text: I’ll first inspect the STEP header and import the assembly with OCCT/build123d, then report its declared units, solid count, validity, and extents before choosing the external-flow meshing strategy.

The import succeeded and found three solids, but validity is a property in this installed build123d version rather than a method. I’ll rerun the inspection in a self-contained corrected cell and search the full STEP text for its unit entities.

The file declares metres, while OCCT’s STEP reader has converted the coordinates into its millimetre working convention: the device is about 53.95 × 46.29 × 31.30 mm, consistent with a lidar. I’ll now make a preview of all three imported bodies so the flow direction and defeaturing approach are based on the actual assembly.

The imported geometry is a compact lidar with a rectangular housing, top cylindrical scanner, and mounting feet. I will take +X as downstream (an explicit assumption because the request does not specify wind direction), use a Cartesian background mesh and snappyHexMesh for the external air, and target a coarse 8 mm base cell with local refinement near the device. Before meshing, I’ll inventory curved faces so only genuinely sub-cell fillets are removed, without rebuilding the design.

The curved-face inventory shows several very small cylindrical and spline details on the scanner body. I’ll measure their analytic radii and extents; this distinguishes small fillets from intentional cylinders such as the scanner and mounting bosses.

The scanner has 0.5 mm blend faces (toruses and adjoining cylindrical transition faces), far below the planned 2 mm finest coarse-grid cell; it also has three 0.1 mm cylindrical engraving/groove faces, which are details rather than fillets. I’ll use OCCT’s defeaturing operator on the 0.5 mm blend faces only, leaving intentional cylinders and markings untouched unless the mesher naturally omits them.

OCCT exposes the needed defeaturing API. I’ll apply it to the six measured 0.5 mm blend faces on the scanner, then validate and compare face count, volume, and bounds to ensure the operation removes details rather than altering the main envelope.
The OCCT defeaturing operation is still running; I’ll wait for that existing operation rather than queueing another cell.
The single OCCT operation has not returned yet. I’ll give it one more longer wait; if it completes, its printed validity comparison will determine whether to retain the defeatured result.
The defeaturing call is abnormally slow for six faces and has produced no result. I’ll wait once more for the in-flight kernel call; no meshing step can safely be queued behind it.
The OCCT call remains in flight; I’ll make the final permitted wait for it to return.

The kernel is still blocked in OCCT with about two minutes of execution allowance left. I’ll wait for the active call to terminate so its final state can be assessed rather than falsely claiming a mesh.

The geometry was inspected successfully, but the OCCT defeaturing operation hung for the remainder of the execution budget before any mesh could be created. I cannot truthfully declare this case complete.
